extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly — scientists, educated public, and professionals interested in book/research notices
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for reviewing scientific books, reports, and tracts for a general-scientific monthly: assessing authoritativeness, methods, evidence, pedagogy, and usefulness to intended audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity and fullness of statements (bank trustworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The utmost publicity and fullness in the statements of condition, and the greatest freedom for the inspection of accounts and securities by depositors, or those in their interest, would contribute much to [banks'] trustworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To convince the public of trustworthiness, managers should provide full, public statements of condition and allow free inspection of accounts and securities by depositors or their representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's qualifications and fitness to treat topic
rubrics_metrics.description: An author should be specially prepared by education and training to investigate the subject and, ideally, be 'to the manner born' — i.e., thoroughly familiar with the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise is due when the author combines formal training with natural suitability for the subject; this lends authority to investigations and conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency and representativeness of data (sample size / response rate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions are hampered by a small number of individuals subjected to analysis; e.g., low response rates to circulars (268 of 1,000) limit ability to generalize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistical findings must be judged against sample size and response bias; small N and low response rates reduce confidence and should temper claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of obtaining data on healthy subjects (methodological limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collecting facts concerning women well is impeded by social delicacy; the inability to gather data on healthy populations affects the evidence base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should note when social or practical barriers bias sampling toward sick populations, and how that limits inferences about the healthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate selection and operationalization of measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of measures (e.g., using the term 'pain' as a well-understood proxy for incapacity) affects interpretation of disability and rest needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should justify operational definitions; reviewers should point out when a chosen term simplifies complex causes (nervous depression, mental disturbance) and the implications of that simplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and presentation of statistical tables and groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts are tabulated under groups distinguished by absence or presence of pain at various periods; ingenious but legitimate use of figures can be hampered by small numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should examine how data are grouped and whether tabulation choices appropriately reflect variability and permit valid inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal inference and directionality (avoiding reversed cause-effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious in inferring cause from association (e.g., lack of occupation may be explained by incapacity due to pain rather than occupation causing pain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review should flag instances where the author may have reversed cause and effect and recommend alternative explanations consistent with the data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of confounding factors (family history vs occupation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data showing family history exerts greater influence over menstrual life than occupation indicate need to account for heredity and other confounders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should analyze and discuss confounders; reviewers should highlight when such factors are overlooked or inadequately controlled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design adequacy (physiological tests require sufficient N)
rubrics_metrics.description: Physiological experiments (e.g., dynamometer, temperature, urea excretion) always require a sufficient number of subjects to reduce individual peculiarities and accidental conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small-sample physiological studies should be treated as preliminary; reviewers should call for larger samples before broad conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate interpretation of physiological measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations (e.g., increased urea excretion prior to hemorrhage, arterial tension changes on sphygmograph) must be interpreted with caution due to individual variability and limited cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overgeneralize from trends with many exceptions; recommend further replication and avoidance of sweeping metaphors (e.g., 'pregnancy in miniature') where unsupported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical consistency and avoidance of self-contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: An author should avoid reasoning against her own convictions or making conclusions that conflict with earlier statements (e.g., asserting menstruation does not imply need for rest while attributing pain to excessive or ill-arranged work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should point out internal contradictions and ask for reconciliation of arguments with presented data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between empirical observation and speculative physiology
rubrics_metrics.description: Clinical facts (e.g., rest quiets pelvic pain) should not be reasoned away by speculative physiology; empirical experience carries weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor conclusions grounded in clinical observation and acknowledge when speculative explanations overreach the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful deliberation in data collection and argumentation (avoid haste)
rubrics_metrics.description: Faults of hasty preparation in both collection of data and arguments can lead to hasty generalizations; wider range of facts and greater deliberation would improve the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should recommend more comprehensive data and more careful argument construction before strong claims are advanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical applicability and audience suitability (tracts for lay use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works intended for practical use (e.g., Fifteen-Cent Dinners) should show how to provide wholesome food within the means of poorly-paid families and be distributed to the target class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess usefulness to intended audience, affordability, clarity of instructions, and efforts for free distribution to those in need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need and clarity of problem statement (navigational accuracy requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports should clearly state the practical need (e.g., improved geographical coordinates for navigation and steamers) motivating the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good report situates the technical work within real-world demands and explains why improved precision matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness and programme uniformity in multi-site operations
rubrics_metrics.description: A comprehensive plan selecting appropriate stations and maintaining absolute uniformity of programme at each station contributes substantially to excellence of results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For multi-station expeditions, reviewers should look for uniform protocols, clear station selection rationale, and consistency across teams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of methods, instruments, and reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Full descriptions of instruments (with plates), methods of observation and reduction should be provided in the volume for particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether technical reports include sufficient methodological detail to permit assessment, replication, or use by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison to standards of excellence (quality benchmarking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Results should be of the same grade of excellence as those attained in similar work of the highest class all over the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess work against state-of-the-art examples; note when methods and results meet, exceed, or fall short of international standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritativeness and trust in textbooks (authority + pedagogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A textbook should be authored by an undoubted authority, be fully trusted, have material well arranged for teaching, and include illustrations and maps that teach general principles by local examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For educational works, evaluate author credentials, organization for instruction, appropriateness of examples, and quality of illustrations/maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining technical rigor with popular accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific monographs should discuss purely scientific and technical aspects with requisite detail while not overlooking 'popular' aspects (life-histories, economic/practical relations) for a larger educated public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good works balance depth for specialists with accessible sections for general readers; reviewers should note inclusion of both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary-source voice and unaffected style (narrative works)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratives relying largely on first-hand words (e.g., accounts 'in the very words' of participants) in a simple, unaffected style are valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess authenticity of voice, fidelity to sources, and clarity of prose; also consider production quality (printing, illustrations, maps) as part of value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative and expert committee composition for standards (pharmacopoeia revision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revision work should be prepared by experts under appropriate control, with representation from chemistry, pharmacognosy, and pharmacy, and the results submitted for criticism to medical and pharmaceutical professions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards-setting requires appropriately composed committees, transparent procedures, and peer criticism; reviewers should note governance and representation issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and management of standard revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals for earlier and more complete revision of standards (e.g., Pharmacopoeia) should address scope, method, suitable managing body, and publication plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether timing and management plans are likely to produce an adequate, accepted standard and whether stakeholder concerns (e.g., pharmacy's share) are addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical report standards (case series reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clinical observations should report number of cases, setting (City Hospital), outcomes (disease arrested within three days), dosing (ten and twenty grain doses), and note of effects (e.g., not antipyretic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case series should include sample size, treatment regimen, time to effect, and side-effect profile; reviewers should judge strength of evidence and caution against overclaiming from small series.
